en: The Sutra on Arousing the Pure Mind, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of Gandhāra in North India during the Sui Dynasty (Sui: Zhìdé).

At that time, the Bhagavān was once again dwelling in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, near the city of Vārāṇasī, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering exactly one thousand, as well as an assembly of five hundred bodhisattvas. Within that assembly, there were many whose faculties were not yet matured, some whose roots of goodness were deficient, and some who possessed karmic obstructions.

At that time, among the bodhisattvas there, there were further bodhisattvas who delighted in worldly affairs, in conversation, in sleep, in miscellaneous occupations, and in frivolous debate; they took pleasure in the distracted activities of various ornate expressions and attachments, which were inconsistent with the practice of dhyāna. They were indolent and lax regarding all virtuous deeds, violated the practice of vigor, lost right mindfulness, lacked any capacity for knowledge, and constantly engaged in distracted conduct.

At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Maitreya, who was seated in that gathering. Having perceived that the bodhisattvas within the assembly were practicing in such a manner, he thought to himself:
"These bodhisattvas are diminishing the factors conducive to the path."
"However, I should now awaken these bodhisattvas and cause them to remember and give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Having formed this thought, at the hour of late afternoon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya arose from meditative concentration and went to where the bodhisattvas were.
Having arrived, he exchanged greetings with those bodhisattvas to comfort them and bring them joy, so as to inspire in them a desire to hear the Dharma.
He then addressed those bodhisattvas, saying: "Venerable ones!..."
"Have you perhaps not diminished [the factors] among the limbs of enlightenment?
After Maitreya Bodhisattva had spoken these words, those bodhisattvas said to Maitreya Bodhisattva,
"Venerable Maitreya!"
Our portion of the path consists only of decline and not of growth.
Why is this so? Because we have taken up and abide in a state of doubt.
"Shall we indeed attain Buddhahood, or shall we not?
Shall we fall into the state of ruin?"
Will they not fall away?
Regarding their roots of goodness, will they arise,
or will they not arise?
"Having conceived such evil thoughts, we remained and grasped these signs.
After they had spoken thus, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed that assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"Venerable ones, you should now go together to the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
However, that Blessed One possesses all-knowing vision and is fully endowed with unimpeded knowledge and liberation; he skillfully knows the mental activities of all sentient beings.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, will gauge your conduct and preach the Dharma for you accordingly.
At that time, sixty bodhisattvas from within that assembly went together with Maitreya Bodhisattva to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived and prostrated themselves with their five limbs at the Buddha’s feet, they did not rise from the ground but wept, shedding tears like rain.
Maitreya Bodhisattva prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“O sons of good family!
"You all should rise; do not weep, do not lament, and do not give way to feverish distress.

You committed these karmic obstructions in the past; at that time, you were filled with joy and exultation, reviling, insulting, and destroying others. You did not believe in the retribution of karma and were unable to discern karmic obstructions, for you were entangled and incompatible with what is wholesome."
At that time, those sixty bodhisattvas bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these words:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
“We pray that you will explain our karmic obstructions in detail, so that we may purify our own minds and not create them again.
When those bodhisattvas had spoken these words, the Buddha addressed those bodhisattvas, saying:
“O sons of good family!

In the past, you all went forth from home to study the Path under the teaching of Krakucchanda Tathāgata; yet once you had gone forth, you remained lax regarding the prohibitions and precepts, remained lax regarding extensive learning, and completely diminished your dhūta merits.
At that time, there were two Dharma-preaching bhikṣus; you slandered them regarding sexual desire.
For the sake of abundant gain and fame, you were envious, stingy, and greedy toward their friends and patrons.

Furthermore, you sowed discord among the lay supporters who were friends of those two Dharma-preachers; through double-tongued speech and insults, you caused them to harbor doubts, so that they would not give rise to faith, their faith would remain incomplete, and you spoke of what was not virtuous.

At that time, for all those sentient beings who gave rise to respectful faith and followed the two Dharma masters, [the demons] caused them to sever their roots of goodness and create various obstacles.
Due to these karmic obstructions, you shall consequently fall into the Avīci Great Hell for sixty-two hundred thousand years;
furthermore, you shall fall into the Saṃjīva Hell for forty thousand years;
and furthermore, you shall fall into the Kālasūtra Hell for twenty thousand years.
Furthermore, for eight hundred thousand years, he fell into the Hot Hell;
thereafter, having passed away from that place and regained a human body, he was born blind and sightless for five hundred lifetimes.

Due to karmic obstructions, wherever they are born, they are entirely dull-witted and forget their original minds; their roots of goodness are blocked, their power is meager, they are abandoned by all, and are constantly subjected to contempt and oppression.
They will be detested by others, subjected to disparagement and slander.

They will always be born in remote regions, impoverished and lowly places, into families of inferior caste; they will receive little material support and little renown, will not be honored or provided for by others, nor will they be respected; they will be disliked by people and loathed by the multitude.

After you have cast off your bodies and lives from this point, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is perishing, you will again be born in a wicked land among wicked people, into a family of low caste, poor and base. You will be slandered by others, lose your original resolve, and have no desire for roots of goodness; you will constantly face obstacles, and though you may briefly encounter light, you will once again be shrouded in darkness.

After those five hundred years, all your karmic obstructions will be completely extinguished; thereafter, you shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the realm of Amitābha, where that Tathāgata will then bestow upon you the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, those sixty persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, having heard this, wiped away their tears; with their hair standing on end from fear, they joined their palms toward the Buddha and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."

From this day forward, if we should give rise to anger or faults toward those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, or further create other karmic obstructions, we now confess them all before the World-Honored One.
“World-Honored One!
We now, before the Tathāgata, make this true vow:
‘World-Honored One!’”
"From this day forward, if we should discover and speak of the transgressions of those persons belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata."
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, if we should mock, despise, or treat with contempt any person (pudgala) who has set out in the bodhisattva vehicle, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward, if we should give rise to pride toward any person (pudgala) who has set out in the bodhisattva vehicle, and speak of their faults—whether true or false—we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward, whenever we see individuals belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle—whether they be householders or renunciants—enjoying the wealth, pleasures, games, and amusements that are the karmic fruits of the five desires, [we shall regard them as such].”

Having seen these things, if one gives rise to a lack of faith, seizes upon their faults, fails to produce a heart of reverence, and does not regard them as teachers, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward, if we—due to the circumstances of begging at the homes of relatives or friends—should cause distress to the body or mind of any person belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, if we should utter sounds of displeasure or sounds of abuse toward any person who practices the Bodhisattva vehicle, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward, if we do not pay homage to any person belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle during the three periods of the day and the three periods of the night, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, if we do not sacrifice either our bodies or our lives to protect these precepts we have received, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward, if we should give rise to thoughts of superiority or self-aggrandizement toward any person belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, we would then be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, while we are wandering, if we do not adopt a humble mind—like that of a caṇḍāla or like a dog—and if we do not act in such a manner, then we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, if we should praise ourselves or disparage others, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, out of fear of anger and strife, if we do not distance ourselves from them by a hundred yojanas as if blown by the wind, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!

From this day forward, regarding those who uphold the precepts, whether they be those of great learning, those with the merit of *dhūta* practices, those who minimize their affairs, or those with other virtues—if we do not praise and speak of them, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, if we do not conceal our own merits and reveal our own faults, we would be deceiving the Tathāgata.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those sixty individuals who had set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle,
saying: "Excellent, excellent,
sons of good family!"
"You have well spoken these various vows; you are able to awaken yourselves and have skillfully made such aspirations.
If you abide in this manner, you shall exhaust all karmic obstructions and attain the purity of the roots of goodness."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: “Maitreya!
If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to purify karmic obstructions, they should make this vow.”
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there any son of good family who, by upholding this vow, shall attain fulfillment and non-retrogression?”
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"There are bodhisattvas who accept and practice this vow; those good sons and good daughters would rather sacrifice their own bodies and lives than fail in this practice, nor would they ever retreat or abandon it."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How many dharmas must those persons who practice the bodhisattva vehicle fulfill so that, during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, they may escape without injury or harm?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying:
"There are four dharmas which, when possessed, enable one to avoid injury and harm, and to attain liberation during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish."
What are the four? Not seeking out the faults of others;
not exposing the transgressions committed by individuals belonging to the Bodhisattva Vehicle; [and so forth].
Maitreya, one does not give rise to stinginess toward the homes of spiritual friends or the homes of donors,
and one abandons harsh speech. Maitreya!

This is for those individuals who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle and are endowed with these four dharmas; in the future, during the final five hundred years, they shall not be diminished or harmed, but will attain liberation and escape.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Do not look for faults in others; Do not speak of what is right or wrong in others.
Do not rely on the livelihoods of others; Abandon all harsh words."

"Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which individuals who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle will, during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish and when the bhikṣus have degenerated, remain unhurt and unharmed, and attain liberation."
What are the four? They are:
those who are incompatible with others should be abandoned; one should distance oneself from the great multitude; [and so forth].
Constantly practice in the araṇya;
subduing one's own body is what corresponds to this. Maitreya!

Those individuals who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle and are endowed with these four qualities will, during that later period of five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, be able to remain unharmed and uninjured within themselves, attaining peaceful liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Abandoning all clamor and remaining in extreme seclusion, do not associate with bhikṣus who lack the Dharma.
One should cultivate the araṇya praised by the Buddha; by not clinging to gain, one attains nirvāṇa."

"Therefore, Maitreya! When the final five hundred years arrive, if a bodhisattva wishes to attain liberation without self-destruction or harm, and desires to be freed from all karmic obstructions, they must not associate with those who are defiled or chaotic. They should dwell in *araṇya*, in empty and secluded groves and forests, remaining apart from all unsuitable beings. They should constantly examine themselves and not seek out the faults of others; they should delight in silence and remain in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*. They should give rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings and preach the Dharma for them, without seeking any reward."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Good son!
There are twenty merits in the gift of Dharma; one preaches the Dharma without seeking karmic retribution, and without attachment to gain, offerings, or fame."
What are the twenty?
Attaining right mindfulness;
attaining the supreme and wondrous destination;
One attains excellent right intention;
one attains powerful willpower;
one attains abundant wisdom.
Awaken to the supramundane Prajñāpāramitā;
one should attain few desires;
one should extinguish anger.
One shall extinguish ignorance;
all Māras shall find no opportunity; and one shall be protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
Non-humans shall protect them;
the devas shall grant them strength;
and no enemies whatsoever shall find an opportunity against them.
All their friends and relatives cannot be estranged;
whatever words they utter will certainly be trusted and accepted by others;
and they shall attain fearlessness.
Wherever one acts, there is constant joy;
the wise offer praise;
and the Dharma-gift one practices is always kept in mind by others.

Maitreya! These are the twenty merits obtained by practicing the gift of Dharma without seeking karmic retribution; one abandons gain and fame, harbors no expectations for robes or food and drink, and practices the gift of Dharma constantly, prioritizing the benefit of others.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

A bodhisattva possesses twenty kinds of merit for which they do not seek karmic rewards. When a bodhisattva practices the gift of Dharma for the sake of others, they do not cling to gain or fame, but practice the gift of Dharma frequently, making the benefit of others their primary concern."
What are these twenty? They are:
being able to cause eloquence that has not yet arisen to arise;
and once it has arisen, not losing it.
One attains dhāraṇīs;
one shall attain subtle movement;
and without requiring great effort, one brings extensive benefit to all sentient beings.
With little exertion of effort, one brings great benefit;
one should show reverence and respect toward sentient beings and should always make offerings to them.
One shall attain the secret of body;
one shall attain the secret of speech;
one shall attain the secret of mind.
One transcends the evil realms and all terrors;
at the time of death, the mind attains joy;
and through speaking correctly according to the Dharma, one is able to subdue the arguments of others.
Possessing great majestic power, he is revered by superior beings, let alone by ordinary commoners;
his faculties are fully perfected, such that none can equal him;
his profound resolve is complete, and he has attained śamatha and vipaśyanā.
They are able to practice difficult austerities with undiminished vigor;
they protect the true Dharma and are swiftly able to transcend to the stage of non-retrogression;
and among all practices, they attain abiding in accordance with them.

Maitreya! These are called the twenty kinds of merit; the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-giving seeks no karmic reward, is not attached to gain, offerings, fame, robes, or food and drink, prioritizes benefiting others, and practices the giving of Dharma repeatedly.

“Maitreya! Observe that in the future, during the final five hundred years, how many ignorant individuals belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle will, when practicing the gift of Dharma, hope for a reward with joy, rather than not hoping for a reward?”
He preaches the Dharma to others with the thought of increasing his circle of friends and the number of those who beg from him; thus he practices the gift of Dharma.
Furthermore, he thinks:

"How may I cause both the ordained and the laity to give rise to pure faith and provide me with the necessities of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites? For this reason, he preaches the Dharma to others.

“Maitreya! It is, for example, like a dead snake, a dead dog, or a dead human; in reality, these are foul, loathsome, festering, and impure, such that all people feel revulsion and abandon them, departing from afar.”

"So it is, so it is! Maitreya! In the future final age, there will be Dharma masters who preach the Dharma for others solely seeking karmic rewards; if they receive no wealth or profit, they will feel aversion and experience distress, becoming weary and abandoning their task."
"We have gained no benefit; there is no profit or reward in such a gift of the Dharma.
Since they did not give us robes, food and drink, bedding, or seats, we thought to ourselves:
"For what reason should we undergo exhaustion and suffering therein?"

That person, for the sake of receiving heavy offerings and serving their own body, keeps attendants and disciples, yet does not do so for the sake of the Dharma; they provide no benefit whatsoever to others, yet with deceptive words they falsely manifest such consolation and instruction to the multitude, saying:

"I possess compassion and gather the assembly in accordance with the Dharma; it is not for the sake of wealth or profit, but for the sake of benefiting them, that I go to those cities, towns, villages, and royal households to bring sentient beings to maturity."
"Although they speak these words, their minds are constantly preoccupied only with matters such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
Maitreya! I do not say that the Dharma-giving of those who seek material wealth is pure."
Why is this? For one who seeks a reward, the Dharma is not impartial. "Maitreya!
I do not say that one who hopes for a reward brings sentient beings to maturity. Why is this?
It is impossible for one who has not yet matured themselves to bring others to maturity.

“Maitreya! I do not say that serving with great devotion, making offerings with affection for the body, and gathering various kinds of material things constitutes the work of benefiting others. Why is this?
Because those who serve [only] do so for the sake of their own physical pleasure, they are unable to gather a community or establish the practice. "Maitreya!
I do not say that one who falsely claims to be virtuous is a forest-dweller."
“Maitreya! I do not say that those of meager merit practice few desires.
“Maitreya! [the Buddha continued.]
"I do not say that one who pursues fine food is practicing alms-gathering.
Maitreya! I do not say that one who has few gains is practicing contentment."
I do not say that one who seeks fine clothing is a wearer of rag robes;
I do not say that one who dwells alone because the laity do not recognize him is practicing without entanglement;
I do not say that one who is fond of flattery and deceitfulness has encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
I do not say that one who seeks out the faults of others is in accord with the Dharma;
I do not say that one who is full of anger has a pure aggregate of precepts;
I do not say that one who is arrogant and conceited possesses great learning.
I do not say that one who forms close cliques is a Vinaya-holder;
I do not say that one whose deportment is turbid is a teacher of the Dharma who is well-revered;
I do not say that one who indulges much in frivolous speech and jesting is a skillful teacher of the Dharma.
I do not say that one who is attached to a household is a teacher of the pure holy life;
I do not say that one who seeks a field of merit for the sake of giving does not hope for a reward;
I do not say that one who seeks the repayment of gratitude is practicing the skillful means of gathering disciples.
I do not say that those who seek gain and fame possess purity of mind;
I do not say that those who lack faith and engage in much conceptual proliferation have truly gone forth;
I do not say that those who merely follow the teachings of others are excellent at maintaining the precepts.
I do not say that one who lacks respect is listening to the Dharma;
I do not say that one who recites worldly treatises and incantations is loving the Dharma;
I do not say that one who does not believe in emptiness attains liberation.
I do not say that one who is stained by attachment is practicing purity;
I do not say that one who acts with attachment is fulfilling the factors of enlightenment;
I do not say that one who dwells in what has been attained is realizing wisdom.
I do not say that being physically weak constitutes fulfillment through patience;
I do not say that being untouched by others constitutes the armor of the power of patience;
I do not say that having few afflictions by nature constitutes purity of precepts.
I do not say that one who speaks much is practicing according to the teaching;
I do not say that one who delights in verbal discourse possesses a single-minded focus;
I do not say that one who delights in worldly occupations does not diminish in the Dharma.
I do not say that one whose inner mind is pure will fall into the evil destinies;
I do not say that one who practices in reliance on wisdom engages in mixed conduct;
I do not say that one who practices in accordance with skillful means is characterized by deceit and crookedness.
I do not say that those who do not seek fame or profit are speaking falsely;
I do not say that those who are free from conceptual proliferation are slandering the Dharma;
I do not say that those who delight in protecting the True Dharma are attached to their own bodies and lives.
"I do not say that those who practice with fear are capable of generating diligence. Maitreya!

Such various faults as flattery, crookedness, perversion, greed, and indulgence will exist; five hundred years after my passing in the future age, those belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle who abide in these evil practices must be guarded against."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Are there only these sixty bodhisattvas who will have various karmic obstructions in the future age after five hundred years, or will there be other bodhisattvas as well?”
The Buddha said, “Maitreya!

After five hundred years, there will be other bodhisattvas who will be ensnared by karmic obstructions; among them, some will be able to exhaust their karmic obstructions, while others will cause them to increase.”
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
Among those five hundred bodhisattvas at that time, there will be twenty bodhisattvas who, in future ages, will have but few karmic obstructions and subtle karmic obstructions."

In the final five hundred years, they shall be born into families of great wealth and noble lineage within villages, towns, cities, and even perilous lands; they will be intelligent and highly wise, skillfully understanding expedient means, with minds that are harmonious, supple, and full of moisture; they will bring vast benefit, being upright and pleasing to behold, possessing subtle eloquence while concealing their own virtues, and abiding in the practice of the dhūta ascetic virtues.
Having accumulated *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* over countless billions of *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they have upheld the True Dharma at the cost of their own bodies and lives.

Dwelling in forest hermitages far removed from villages, they do not seek fame or profit but always delight in diligent effort. They enter into the conduct of sentient beings and are skilled in discourse; they master worldly treatises and understand much from hearing little. They are fully adept at *vipaśyanā* (insight), possess eloquence, and are skilled in discernment; they can answer questions according to their inquiries in a manner consistent with the meaning, having attained unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, there may be those who have attained the inexhaustible dharani; when they expound the Dharma for the fourfold assembly, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and through the Buddha’s sustaining support, they are able to explain and discourse upon the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-kathās, vaipulyas, adbhuta-dharmas, and upadeśas taught by the Tathāgata.

“Maitreya! At that time, those twenty bodhisattvas skilled in expedient means received from their preceptors, such as Upādhyāya and others, these immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sūtra passages of this Dharma-text, and they all recited, maintained, and explained them.”
"Because he recites and upholds this Dharma-text, that son of good family will dwell with a mind free from doubt or regret regarding all forms of eloquence, having fully embraced it.
Furthermore, Maitreya!"

At that time, there will also be bodhisattvas lacking skillful means—whether they be lay householders or ordained monastics—who, toward those who uphold the true Dharma, those who practice the teachings, and those who practice according to reality, as well as toward those Dharma-preachers, will not accept or uphold the Dharma-teachings they proclaim. Instead, they will deceive and mock them, saying:
"You yourselves have fabricated these teachings; the phrases of the Dharma you preach were not spoken by the Tathāgata.

You have assembled these literary ornaments according to your own whims and bound yourselves to one another with them. We do not give rise to reverence for this Dharma, nor do we conceive of it as something rare and difficult to encounter."

“Maitreya! At that time, there will be many sentient beings who slander this Dharma, destroy this Dharma, and refuse to accept this Dharma, treating it as if it were the playful antics of a performer. They will associate with such people, saying:
‘These bhikṣus do not rely on the Sūtras nor the Vinaya when they expound the words of the Dharma.’”
"You should not give rise to a mind of reverence, faith, or wonder, for this is not the True Dharma. "Maitreya!

Those foolish people do not know that all these well-spoken words are taught by the Tathāgata. Possessed by Māra, those people will give rise to slander against the Dharma spoken by those Dharma-preachers, and they will create the karmic causes and conditions for slandering the Dharma."
Because of the causal conditions of having committed the karma of slandering the Dharma, one shall fall into the evil realms.

Therefore, Maitreya, a bodhisattva who wishes to protect the True Dharma should employ skillful means to conceal their own virtues; they must provide protection for sentient beings engaged in various practices, ensuring that such beings do not give rise to thoughts of obstruction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One! Bhagavān!”

At that time, those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle will lack wisdom and fail to seek eloquence; unable to give rise to faith in persons or dharmas, from whom could they possibly seek to cultivate roots of goodness?
One should seek dhāraṇīs for one's own protection;
otherwise, one will give rise to slander and impurity toward those Dharma-preachers who uphold the Dharma.
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a person who, thirsty and wishing to drink water, went to a spring, a pond, a marsh, or a well; yet before drinking the water, he first threw excrement and filth into it. Having thrown the filth in, he wished to drink the water again, but upon smelling its foul stench, he loathed it and would not drink. Rather than explaining the cause of his own defilement, he instead spoke of the fault of the other, saying: ‘How strange!’”
"This water is extremely foul and filthy.
Thus, failing to recognize his own transgression, he attributes the fault to that water. "It is so, it is so!"
“World-Honored One!

Those foolish people seek the Dharma throughout the long night and desire to examine its practice; yet, having first sought out faults in persons and dharmas, they subsequently develop hatred for the Dharma-preacher and the Dharma he teaches upon hearing it. Just as those fools loathe springs, pools, ponds, wells, and lakes, so should the bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma understand them.”
If there are those who can preach this Dharma, you should know that it is entirely due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
“It is so, World-Honored One!

After five hundred years have passed, there will be ignorant bodhisattvas who, having defiled both that Dharma and the bhikṣus who uphold it, yet wish to drink the flavor of the Dharma from their very side. They do not perceive their own faults and evils; instead, they will mock those Dharma masters, proclaiming their transgressions before the assembly. Having given rise to defilement, they seek out their shortcomings; having conceived feelings of aversion, they then wish to abandon them.”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!”
"You have spoken these words well.
If one does not seek out the faults or shortcomings of others, one should know that one is not free from all faults and evils oneself, Maitreya."
There are four causes and conditions by which all eloquence spoken by the Buddhas should be understood.

Maitreya, furthermore, there are four causes and conditions by which you should know that the four types of eloquence are censured by all the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, and are not approved by any of the Buddhas.
Maitreya! What are the causes and conditions for the four analytical knowledges?
You should know that they are what all Buddhas have taught.

Maitreya! That eloquence is endowed with meaning and not devoid of meaning; it is endowed with the Dharma and not devoid of the Dharma. It should exhaust afflictions rather than increase them, and it proclaims the merits of Nirvana while demonstrating the faults and evils of saṃsāra.
"Maitreya! These are the four analytical knowledges; you should understand them as that which is taught by all Buddhas. Maitreya!"

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who, being endowed with and corresponding to these four analytical knowledges, are able to expound them, then any son of good family or daughter of good family should regard such a person as the Buddha and as their teacher while listening to the meaning of the Dharma.
Why is this? Maitreya!
You should know that whatever is spoken by them is all spoken by the Tathāgata; you should view it in this way.
“Maitreya! If there are those who slander these four analytical knowledges, saying:
‘These were not spoken by the Buddha.’”
Because they do not give rise to a mind of respect and reverence, and instead harbor hatred and envy toward others, they slander the eloquence spoken by all Buddhas.
Having slandered the Dharma, they commit the karma of destroying the Dharma;
having committed the act of destroying the Dharma, they fall into the evil realms.

Therefore, Maitreya! If there are sons of good family with faith who wish to distance themselves from and eliminate the causes and conditions of karmic obstructions regarding the Dharma, they should not harbor hatred toward the Dharma because of their hatred for people; nor should they fail to give rise to a heart of love for that Dharma simply because they do not love certain individuals.
“Maitreya! What kind of eloquent discourse is censured by all Buddhas and not permitted? Maitreya!”

There may be some forms of eloquent discourse that provide no benefit, do not rely on the true Dharma, increase afflictions rather than exhausting them, increase the cycle of birth and death rather than bringing an end to it, and fail to praise the merits and benefits of Nirvana.
“Maitreya! Such a debater is censured by all Buddhas; all Buddhas do not approve of him.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there is eloquence that increases birth and death, it is not the eloquence of a Buddha.
Why, then, does the World-Honored One say that the various afflictions bring benefit to bodhisattvas?”
"Furthermore, do you also praise and explain the cycle of birth and death as being the fulfillment of the factors of enlightenment?
World-Honored One!
Is it not the case that such a discourse was spoken by the Tathāgata?"
The Buddha said to Maitreya: "What do you think?

If these afflictions are taught for the sake of fulfilling the factors of enlightenment and for the benefit of all bodhisattvas, then one must further praise the undergoing of the cycle of birth and death."
Now, as for this matter, is it consistent with the meaning?
Is it inconsistent with the meaning?
Or is it consistent with the Dharma?
"Would this not be contrary to the Dharma? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"If there is one who speaks correctly, whose speech accords with meaning and accords with the Dharma, and if such a person exists, they are called one of correct speech.
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"
For this reason, you should know that everything spoken by all Buddhas is the Buddha’s eloquence; you should view it in this way.

If there is anything said regarding the various afflictions, it is because they fulfill the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa); it is taught for the sake of bodhisattvas so that they may bring about benefit. Furthermore, the praise of those who take up the flow of saṃsāra is for the purpose of benefiting bodhisattvas.
Why is this so? Maitreya!

A bodhisattva who is beset by afflictions should view it in this way: this bodhisattva does not incur the offense of these afflictions, because he has attained mastery over their meaning and has also attained mastery over the dharmas.
This is the skillful means of the bodhisattvas in that regard; it is not the stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Maitreya!
If there were afflictions that provided no benefit, they would not fulfill the causal conditions for the factors of enlightenment, nor would they serve as causes for the gateway of roots of goodness.
In this regard, that bodhisattva should not begrudge his body or life, nor should he succumb to those afflictions.
Why is this? Maitreya!
"If a Bodhisattva who has attained the power of wisdom has a separate object of attachment, it is because they see the existence of afflictions and are separately attached to conditioned phenomena.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if there is a bodhisattva who does not wish to create karmic obstructions, who wishes to exhaust karmic obstructions, and who, being neither deficient nor impaired, desires liberation, that person, at a time in the future age, should have faith in the bodhisattva practice; they must reflect upon it, refrain from seeking the faults of others, constantly seek matters of merit, and seek the place of true reality.
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, Maitreya!”
In future ages, that bodhisattva should contemplate the bodhisattva practice and should understand skillful means.
Why is this? For the wisdom-practice of a bodhisattva who possesses skillful means is difficult to comprehend.

Maitreya! It is like a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) who, while among the practices of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), manifests the stage of a stream-enterer. He is distinct from ordinary worldlings and distinct in his afflictions; whereas those ordinary worldlings—driven by desire, hatred, and delusion—are destined to fall into the evil realms, that noble disciple of the *śrāvaka* does not fall into the evil realms because he has realized this for himself. Thus it is.
Maitreya! It is so, it is so!

Because the bodhisattva practicing wisdom has not yet exhausted the defilements of habitual delusions, there is a distinct stage for him; the bodhisattva at the initial stage of practice likewise has a distinct stage.

Why is this? Because his mind does not dwell upon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), whereas ordinary worldlings are defiled by and attached to these latent tendencies; due to the causes and conditions of ignorance, they are unable to skillfully know the place of liberation.

“Maitreya! Although a bodhisattva practicing with wisdom may have grave offenses, by the power of wisdom they shall be completely consumed like ashes; nor shall they fall into the evil realms because of them.”
Maitreya! It is like a blazing fire into which one repeatedly throws large logs of wood; as they are thrown in again and again, the fire grows ever more intense and does not go out.
"It is so, it is so, Maitreya!

When the fire of wisdom blazes intensely within a bodhisattva practicing wisdom, they cast the afflictions of the conditioned into that fire of wisdom; thus, the fire of wisdom blazes even more fiercely and cannot be extinguished, by virtue of the power of wisdom."
“Maitreya! By this you should know that the conduct of those bodhisattvas who practice with wisdom is difficult to comprehend.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For a beginner bodhisattva who has not yet attained the power of wisdom and has left home to renounce the world, which dharmas should be abandoned?
Which dharmas should be cultivated?”
"If one associates with those bodhisattvas, the power of wisdom that has not yet arisen will be caused to arise, and that which has already arisen will be caused to increase and not diminish.
The Buddha said, "Maitreya!"

When a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice leaves home for the homeless life and has not yet attained the power of wisdom, although they have renounced material wealth and the acts of making offerings, they must contemplate the various afflictions of gain and fame; they must quickly abandon worldly talk and contemplate the faults of worldly talk; they must abandon the delight in speaking much and contemplate the faults of speaking much; they must abandon the delight in sleep and contemplate the faults of sleep; they must abandon the delight in performing various activities and contemplate the faults of worldly activities; they must abandon the delight in play and contemplate the faults of the delight in play.
Having abandoned gain, offerings, and fame, one must practice fewness of desires and contentment, and must associate with those who possess fewness of desires and contentment;
having abandoned worldly talk, one must associate with those who delight in solitary practice;
and having abandoned excessive speech, one must contemplate the true meaning.
Having abandoned sleep, one must remain alert throughout the first and last watches of the night;
having abandoned the pleasure of engaging in worldly activities, one must draw near to the supramundane Dharma;
and having abandoned the pleasure of play, one should cultivate the compassion that finds no sentient beings.

Maitreya! A bodhisattva who has first set out on the path, having left home for the homeless life, and who has not yet attained the power of wisdom but desires to attain it, must abandon such dharmas as these and must cultivate such dharmas as these.

“Maitreya! For that beginner bodhisattva who has left home for the homeless life but has not yet attained the power of wisdom—so long as they have not yet abandoned gain and fame, and have not yet drawn near to those who possess few desires and are content—it is impossible for them to give rise to the power of wisdom if it has not yet arisen, or to cause it to increase if it has already arisen.”

If one has not yet abandoned worldly talk, has not yet cultivated solitary wandering, does not relinquish the pleasure of sleep, and fails to apply oneself to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night to practice wholesome deeds, then it is impossible for them to cultivate supramundane dharmas during that time; it is impossible for them to abandon playfulness, to cultivate the thought of compassion toward all beings, or to give rise to the power of wisdom where it has not yet arisen, or to increase it where it has already arisen.

“Maitreya! Therefore, if there is a bodhisattva who wishes to give birth to the power of wisdom, that bodhisattva should abandon all dharmas that ought to be abandoned, and should practice and cultivate all dharmas that ought to be cultivated and approached.”
Why is this so? Maitreya!
Wisdom arises from causes; without causes, wisdom cannot arise.
"Because the conditions are not in harmony, it is impossible for birth to occur.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How should a bodhisattva contemplate the faults and afflictions of gain and fame?
What are these various afflictions of gain and fame such that, when a bodhisattva contemplates them, they should delight in contentment and remain free from regret?
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"In this regard, a bodhisattva should contemplate gain and offerings so as not to give rise to desire.

By contemplating in this way, one avoids the harm caused by the arising of desire due to gain and offerings, which damages one's own practice and gives rise to mental resentment and various afflictions."
One should contemplate that gain gives rise to delusion and folly, for it engenders pride;
one should contemplate that gain gives rise to envy and jealousy;
one should contemplate that gain gives rise to the cultivation of deceitful illusions and the attachment to their flavors.
One should contemplate that gain and sustenance give rise to flattery and crookedness;
one should contemplate that gain and sustenance cause one to depart from the four noble lineages;
one should contemplate that gain and sustenance bring no sense of shame, for they are not permitted by any of the Buddhas.

One should contemplate that gain and sustenance give rise to self-conceit and arrogance, leading one not to feel love or respect toward the Venerable Ones, for such a person is not remembered by anyone;
one should contemplate that gain and sustenance assist the various Māras, being the sole root of heedlessness;
one should contemplate that gain and sustenance crush all roots of goodness, just like rain and hail.
One should contemplate that gain and offerings are full of various impurities;
one should contemplate that gain and offerings cause the loss of the homes of spiritual friends and companions;
and one should contemplate that gain and offerings can give rise to love and hatred, as well as sorrow and affliction.
One should contemplate that gain and offerings disturb the foundations of mindfulness because they cause much defilement;
one should contemplate that gain and offerings weaken the pure dharmas because they cause a deficiency in right effort;
one should contemplate that gain and offerings constitute the greatest obstacle because they prevent the attainment of the various supernormal powers.
One should contemplate that gain and offerings involve deception and fraud, as they lead each person to speak of unwholesome matters;
one should contemplate that gain and offerings give rise to much discrimination, for they cause one to deliberate and create karma;
one should contemplate that gain and offerings distance one from all forms of happiness, for they cause the loss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the attainments (*samāpatti*).
One should contemplate gain and offerings as being like a courtesan, for they cause wisdom to become agitated and lead one away from seclusion;

one should contemplate how gain and offerings cause one to fall into the evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, as was the case with Devadatta and Udraka who heard and practiced [the teachings].
“Maitreya! A bodhisattva should observe gains and offerings in this way.
Having observed them thus, when one contemplates in this manner, the inclination of the mind will be toward few desires, and one will be able to remain free from regret.”
Why is this so? Maitreya!

A bodhisattva with few desires is free from such faults and afflictions; he shall become a vessel for the Buddhadharma, not subject to the deception or arrogance of either the ordained or the laity. He will attain pure faith without fear, remain unafraid of any evil realms, and never be overcome by them. He will distance himself from all attachment to sensory flavors, transcend the realms of Māra, and attain liberation. He will be praised by all Buddhas, cherished by devas and humans, and remain unstained by the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

Because of such intimacy, one should give rise to joy and abandon deceit; one should not be negligent, but observe the perils of the five desires. As one’s speech does not differ from one’s actions, one dwells within the lineage of the noble ones, constantly observing as a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Maitreya! A wise Bodhisattva, contemplating such merits as these, should distance himself from gain and fame, dwell with a right mind in contentment, and extinguish all craving and desire.
Having spoken these words, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva contemplate the faults and afflictions of worldly speech?"
"What are the afflictions of worldly discourse?
Rather, the Bodhisattva, having contemplated this, delights in solitary practice and feels no regret.
The Buddha replied:
“Maitreya! There are twenty kinds of afflictions in worldly discourse that must be contemplated; when a bodhisattva contemplates them, he delights in solitary practice.
What are these twenty?
Not guarding one's bodily conduct;
not guarding one's verbal conduct;
not guarding one's mental conduct.
There will be those who engage in various sensual desires;
there will be many who harbor ill will;
and there will be many who are deluded.
They engage extensively in worldly discourse,
while diminishing discourse concerning the supramundane;
they associate with those who do not respect the Dharma.
They will distance themselves from the True Dharma;
Māra will find his opportunity;
they shall practice heedlessness.
Causing one to incline toward negligence;
abounding in conceptual proliferation;
and regarding extensive learning as diminished.
One will be unable to attain śamatha and vipaśyanā;
one will quickly fail to accomplish the holy life (brahmacarya);
and one’s faith in the Buddha will diminish.
"Maitreya, regarding the decline of faith in the Dharma and the Saṅgha—
these twenty worldly discourses concerning afflictions— if a bodhisattva contemplates such things as these, he will delight in solitary practice without becoming weary."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Abandoning the precepts and distancing oneself from tranquility, If one delights in worldly talk,
Such defiled attachment leads toward the breaking of the precepts."
Furthermore, there are such faults as frivolity, excessive laughter, and discursive thought.
They engage in such worldly talk; they will surely have mixed conduct and lack self-restraint.
The ignorant delight in worldly knowledge and its doctrines; lacking wisdom, they diminish sublime discourse, increasing negligence and prolific conceptualization.
If one engages in worldly conversation, [these faults arise].
This also does not increase one's learning;
it is incompatible with discourse on the arising of joy;
and it constantly diminishes all meditative concentrations.
What stability can there be in worldly reflection? Without attaining tranquil concentration, one lacks right contemplation;
therefore, for such a person, there is no superior holy life.
They harbor no heart of reverence toward the Buddha, nor do they hold the noble Saṅgha in esteem.
I abandoned those most supreme and excellent dharmas;
in the past, I sacrificed my body thousands of times for the sake of seeking the conditions for unsurpassed bodhi,
never growing weary of hearing the true Dharma.
They shall abandon diligence and cease their efforts; they take no pleasure in sons, daughters, wives, or concubines.
In the past, I renounced my throne and all my wealth for the sake of a single four-line verse; why, then, would the wise not listen to the Dharma?
One should renounce everything in every place, and likewise avoid engaging in defiled speech;
such a person finds no delight in the sublime Dharma, for one who achieves it is difficult to find even in a hundred kalpas.
If you wish to attain liberation, cultivate merit; do not inquire about worldly affairs.
That which does not lead to self-benefit or nirvana, nor is for the sake of food and clothing—if one asks such things, they may be considered superior and worthy of praise.
I have prepared a seat for you; come and sit. Each of you should speak of your Dharma practice:
having well obtained this human body so difficult to find, have you increased your wholesome qualities (*śukladharma*)?
While engaged in recitation and various meditative concentrations, a bhikṣu should pose such questions:
"After the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, will there be the destruction and ruin of the Dharma teachings?"

There were certain bhikṣus who lacked dignified deportment; they delighted in the assembly and abandoned the forest hermitage (araṇya), constantly discussing gain, wealth, robes, and the like day and night.
While sleeping and unmoving in a dream, one sees plowing and crops;
when ordinary people realize they have lost these things, they are born into the three miserable realms of the evil paths.
Having given rise to joy and exultation, one should dwell in the forest like a rhinoceros;
dwelling in an araṇya for the sake of seeking bliss, one should not, at that time, perceive the faults of others.

"I am the foremost among the most excellent assembly"—one should not give rise to such a thought, for this is the root of arrogance and heedlessness; thus, O bhikṣu, do not look down upon others with contempt.
In this Dharma teaching, one cannot attain liberation all at once;
even if one sees a bhikṣu who has broken the prohibitions, one should still have faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Do not seek out the faults and afflictions of others; this [restraint] serves as the cause for their liberation.
Since the various desires and hatreds are difficult to restrain, do not be negligent regarding mastery over them.
While one has not yet attained the cultivation of all dharmas, do not abandon them by breaking the precepts;
if one lets the mind of diligence cease and fails to exert oneself, this is most truly called being "one who does not advance."
Practicing diligence, one does not see the faults of others; by contemplating the right path, one is liberated from suffering.
Therefore, a bhikṣu who seeks virtue should abandon unwholesome speech.
Having applied himself with diligent effort and leaping with joy, he should dwell in seclusion like a rhinoceros.
*The Sutra on Arousing the Pure Mind*, Volume Upper and Volume Lower,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of Gandhāra in North India during the Sui Dynasty.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare, World-Honored One!
When people of the world gather for conversation, there are so many such defiled faults and afflictions, with no harmony of merit whatsoever."
These worldly conversations merely increase the various afflictions and should be treated as false within the context of the pure dharmas.
World-Honored One,
what wise bodhisattva seeking merit would, upon hearing such words concerning the faults of the world, not take pleasure in practicing alone?
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva delight in much speech while also contemplating its faults?
When a bodhisattva contemplates in this way, he delights in discerning the true meaning, and thereafter has no regrets.
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! Among these, a bodhisattva should contemplate twenty kinds of faults regarding those who delight in much talk.”
What are these twenty? Maitreya,
one who delights in much talk will lack a mind of reverence because of their extensive learning;
With pride and negligence, one will become attached to speech and thought;
one will lose one's original mindfulness and lack self-rectifying awareness;
one's actions will be improper in their deportment, and one will be unable to subdue body and mind.
In whatever place they travel, their bodies are not upright; they have lost patience regarding the Dharma;
their bodies and minds are rigid and difficult to bend;
and they are far removed from *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
They do not know the proper timing for their speech, and their words are foul and turbid;
they will be greedy for food and drink,
and they shall not attain noble wisdom.
They will not be respected by the devas, nāgas, and others;
whatever eloquence they may obtain will always be held in contempt;
and they shall constantly feel regret in the future.
Not abiding in correctness, one's conduct shall be flighty and restless;
unable to extinguish or sever various doubts, when acting, one is like Nala who merely follows after sounds;
one should conform to the merits of all desires, and consciousness flows along in accordance with them.
They slander the true Dharma because they do not contemplate reality as it is;

they repeatedly give rise to what they desire, moving where they should remain still and remaining still where they should move; they fail to receive the offerings they deserve because their minds are not disciplined;
and they are led astray by others because they have not penetrated the dharma-realm.
Because they are led astray by various afflictions and their faculties are not subdued,
Maitreya, bodhisattvas who delight in much talk have these twenty kinds of faults; they merely believe in and know sounds, but do not contemplate the true meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Though learned, they are like the intoxicated, lacking a heart of reverence; They dwell in reliance upon restless and confused speech.
Forgetting right mindfulness and lacking right wisdom— Such are the afflictions of one who delights in much talk."
Internally reflecting, one finds it exceedingly distant; the body lacks tranquility and the mind is likewise so.
One's movements—bending, bowing, contracting, and extending—are impaired; such are the afflictions of delighting in much speech.
One who forgets the intent through reflecting on the True Dharma possesses only a parched and rigid mind devoid of moisture;
having abandoned both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* in meditative concentration, such a person suffers from the affliction of delighting in much talk.
The Venerable Sañjīva lacks respect; he constantly delights in contentious speech.
Dwelling with an unstable and perverted mind, he takes pleasure in much talk—such are his afflictions.
The hosts of devas will not show him respect, nor will the nāgas and yakṣas keep him in mind;
later, he will possess no eloquence—such are the afflictions of one who delights in much talk.
The wise always reproach those who merely claim they should realize [the truth] within their own bodies;
their lives are empty and of no benefit, for they delight in much talk—such is their affliction.
When that deluded one passes away, they will feel regret, thinking: "I have been deceived; what can I say now?
They shall experience manifold sufferings as a consequence of their fondness for much talk; such is the affliction of excessive speech.
Fickle as grass blown by the wind, harboring doubts that cannot be resolved,
lacking firm resolve and unable to attain stability— such are the afflictions of one who delights in much speech.
Just as Nata performs on the stage, proclaiming his own heroic virtues, so too at that time is he like Nata; such is the affliction of delighting in much talk.
When one hears pleasant sounds with a defiled mind, that craving for sound distances one from right knowledge;
just as there is improper reflection on the wrong path, such is the affliction of delighting in excessive speech.

Such a person will be deceitful and utterly hopeless; repeatedly giving rise to disputes and contention, they remain farthest from the noble practices—such are the afflictions of one who delights in much speech.
Their actions are conditioned and their mindfulness lacks stability; when others inquire of their noble virtue, they are always fickle and restless.
Like the agitated mind of a monkey, they delight in much speech—such is their affliction.
That deluded person is driven by others; lacking self-knowledge and right concentration, he is followed and aided by various afflictions—such is the calamity of delighting in much speech.
It will disorder his eyes, ears, and nose; his tongue, body, and mind shall likewise be disordered.
All his faculties will function in total confusion—such is the affliction of delighting in excessive speech.
Though the ignorant seek many words and pursue all dharmas with tireless intent, they shall not receive the Dharma of joy;
their minds find no delight even for a single thought-moment.
The skin of the sugarcane stalk is not firm, yet the flavor within its heart is supreme;
one does not extract flavor by crushing the skin, for that flavor is inseparable from the sugarcane itself.
Just as it is with the many words of the bark, so too is it with contemplating the meaning of the juice;
therefore, delight in being far removed from much talk, contemplate the true meaning, and do not be negligent.
The flavor of meaning and the flavor of the Dharma surpass all others; the flavor of liberation is likewise sublime.
This is the supreme flavor among all flavors; why, then, would the wise not practice alone?
Having thus understood the many words, and knowing this most excellent merit of the ultimate meaning,
any wise person who wishes to train in the Path should contemplate that true reality.
Therefore, one should distance oneself from useless speech;
those who seek the supreme truth of suchness must approach the most excellent Dharma and abide therein to realize the sublime path.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!
You have been able to skillfully explain the faults and afflictions of excessive speech."
World-Honored One!
Contemplating the true meaning possesses great merit.
World-Honored One!
If one wishes to seek the meaning of firmness, a bodhisattva who desires to don the armor and weapons of the sword should not delight in practicing deceptive speech.
World-Honored One,
how could a bodhisattva delight in sleep?
"One should contemplate all afflictions; when a bodhisattva contemplates them, they should abandon sleep, diligently arouse vigor, and not give rise to weariness.
After Maitreya had spoken these words, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya, saying: "Maitreya!"
Within this context, a bodhisattva should contemplate twenty kinds of faults regarding sleep. What are these twenty? Maitreya!
Now, if a bodhisattva were to delight in sleep, they would become indolent, their body heavy, and their skin impure;
their flesh and skin would become coarse and rough,
and the four great elements would become foul and turbid.
Their majestic power and virtue become diminished;
their food and drink are not digested;
and sores and blisters break out upon their bodies.
They are largely indolent;
they increase the net of delusion;
and their wisdom is feeble.
One's wholesome aspirations grow weary;
one shall proceed toward darkness;
and people will show one no respect.
Endowed with a nature of folly and ignorance;
abounding in various afflictions;
and with a mind directed toward the latent tendencies.
They do not generate desire for wholesome dharmas;
they cause all pure dharmas to diminish;
and they constantly act within a state of alarm and fear.
Seeing those who are diligent, they revile and humiliate them;
consequently, when they enter the great assembly, they are treated with contempt by others. Maitreya!
"When a bodhisattva delights in sleep, there are twenty such afflictions as these.
If a bodhisattva contemplates this, they should delight in exerting diligence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The body is heavy and lacks meditative concentration; Laziness and indolence cause the form to be unupright;
The skin is foul and impure, As one follows the inclination toward sleep."
Tears, saliva, wind, and phlegm abound within the body;
when the various elements are disordered and imbalanced, one indulges in the practice of following the inclination toward sleep.
The food he eats does not digest; his body is coarse and lacks luster;
his voice becomes hoarse and broken, as he indulges in the habit of excessive sleep.
The body is rife with various sores and eruptions; for one who follows the habit of sleeping day and night, much suffering arises within the body if they delight in and pursue the practice of sleep.
Many are indolent and have abandoned diligence; they are far removed from all joys and lack a share of wealth.
Constantly intoxicated by sleep, they lack right intention, following the habitual practice of indulging in slumber.
The net of delusion constantly grows, and the various inverted views are extremely difficult to cure;
those who lack right mindfulness are robbed by their own minds, if they delight in sleep and act accordingly.
Their wisdom is exceedingly feeble; all dharmas have declined and they lack meditative concentration.
Having abandoned wisdom and right abiding, they delight in sleep and follow its impulses.
Knowing that such a person is indolent and does not apply themselves to study, their majestic power is constantly snatched away by non-human spirits;
dwelling in an araṇya, they are perpetually terrified, for they delight in sleep and act accordingly.
Constantly muddled and losing right mindfulness, they are unable to remain steadfast in recitation;
they constantly forget the True Dharma they have taught, if they follow the practice of delighting in sleep.
Those who constantly protect and assist their afflictions, who are perpetually distracted and deluded, and whose nature is fickle,
will later give rise to regret if they indulge in the practice of excessive sleep.
When one has many karmas that have been extinguished, Recalling and seeking them brings about distress and regret;
It increases the ground of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and afflictions, If one delights in sleep and acts accordingly.
Having no desire for any wholesome deeds, having no seeking mind regarding any phenomena,
repeatedly practicing what is unrighteous, and following along with a delight in sleep.
This is to distance oneself from the path to enlightenment;
all merits will utterly diminish, and one will be extinguished from the pure state into darkness, if one delights in sleep and acts accordingly.
Lacking fearless and ardent resolve, they never give rise to thoughts of joy;
seized by sloth and indulging in negligence, they delight in following the practice of sleep.
Recognizing his own state of indolence, he envies those who abide in the power of diligence;
he speaks ill of diligence, following instead the inclination toward sleep.
If a wise person perceives such afflictions as these, who would take delight in shared sleep?
It gives rise exclusively to delusion and the dense web of views; it extinguishes the desire for the True Dharma and its merits.
What wise person would not rejoice in diligence?
If one can extinguish suffering and purify all darkness, the evil realms of the future will be entirely exhausted; as the root of all happiness, one attains the nectar of immortality.

Regarding all the arts and skills found in the world, as well as all the capacities for transcending the world, it is not difficult for one who can arouse diligence; why, then, would the wise not exert themselves with vigor?
If you wish to dwell truly in supreme enlightenment, you should recognize the affliction of sleep;
be diligent, untiring, and heedful—I have awakened you to this.
Therefore, being free from negligence and fear, one gives rise to a mind of diligence and meditative concentration;
abandoning all afflictions and departing from sleep, one guards both awakening and its seeds.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Such things ought to be seen by the Tathāgata for the sake of all bodhisattvas; yet, having heard of these many afflictions of excessive sleep, they are still unable to sever them, nor can they give rise to a mind of weary detachment.”
World-Honored One!
Why would a bodhisattva who wishes to train in faith and aspires to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* give rise to indolence?

For the sake of seeking the wholesome dharmas, although one has heard of these many meritorious qualities, one is unable to arouse diligence and put them into practice, desiring instead to fulfill the factors of enlightenment.
The Tathāgata has already well explained the many faults of excessive sleep and the various merits of exerting diligence.

World-Honored One, how should a bodhisattva contemplate the faults of delighting in the creation of various karmas? Once a bodhisattva has so contemplated, they should practice few desires and contentment.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"In this regard, a bodhisattva engaged in the work of pleasure should contemplate twenty kinds of afflictions. What are these twenty?"
Maitreya! It is said that if a bodhisattva delights in performing various worldly activities, they will take pleasure in mundane dharmas and thus abide in all the most inferior of actions;
those who exert themselves in recitation and study will be treated with contempt by others.
All those who exert themselves in solitary meditative concentration shall be mocked by others;
furthermore, from the beginningless flow of saṃsāra until now, they shall continue to create karma without ceasing;
and all those faithful elders shall not be able to serve as fields of merit for them.
They are constantly possessed by greed;
with a mind that craves all things, they direct their actions toward them;
and through the exertion of their efforts, they are perpetually anxious about their household affairs.
They violate the wholesome dharmas of others;
though given instruction in the Dharma, they do not comply;
and they harbor many thoughts of attachment to various flavors.
They take no delight in the refined and sublime things they have obtained;
they constantly engage in the performance of harmful and evil karma;
and toward their spiritual friends, both old and new, they are perpetually preoccupied with thoughts of food and drink.
They constantly delight in knowing the faults, merits, strengths, and weaknesses of others;
they constantly delight in engaging in discordant speech and debate;
and they do not accept the instructions of their fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Constantly observing the faults of others while failing to observe one's own,
one will quickly be held in contempt by others;
furthermore, one’s words will always fall short when engaged in genuine deliberation.
“Maitreya! If a bodhisattva delights in creating various karmic actions, there will be twenty such evil faults and afflictions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Constantly dwelling in base occupations, he is far removed from superior deeds;
within this teaching there is no greatness for one who is preoccupied with worldly affairs."
Those bhikṣus who delight in recitation and study are held in contempt by others and do not inspire admiration;
those who practice meditative concentration abandon them, for such is the affliction of those preoccupied with worldly affairs.

Constantly toiling amidst the karma of birth and death, dwelling far from the state of liberation while bound by all fetters, whatever food one consumes is impure food; such are the afflictions of those engaged in worldly occupations.
Constantly engaging in various activities, they take up all manner of things without weariness;
always craving the objects they receive, those engaged in worldly enterprises suffer from such afflictions.
Clinging with greedy attachment to friends and companions, they engage in mixed conduct together, mutually defiling one another;
like birds caught within a cage, such is the affliction of those engaged in worldly affairs.
Constantly anxious regarding their household affairs, their minds are ever sorrowful and never at ease;
whatever words they utter go unheeded by others—such are the afflictions of those engaged in worldly occupations.

If there are those who teach virtue but do not practice it themselves, and one does not accept the teachings that accord with the Dharma, then their observance of the precepts will be incomplete; such is the affliction of those engaged in worldly affairs.
Constantly sorrowful and with an uneasy mind, they apply their efforts to worldly affairs;
they have no desire for wisdom or tranquility—such is the affliction of those engaged in business.
He is constantly preoccupied with many worldly affairs, bound by various kinds of flavors;
finding no satisfaction anywhere he goes, such is the affliction of one engaged in busywork.
They always delight in the assemblies of others, yet the wise do not enjoy conversing with them;
they take pleasure in filth like a donkey—such is the affliction of those engaged in worldly affairs.
The mind is constantly full of resentment and lacks moisture; it increases all karmic actions without ever ceasing.
Bound and entangled by the firm fetters of craving and defilement—such are the afflictions of those engaged in worldly affairs.
He does not rely upon the venerable ones, but relies upon lay households for assistance;
seeing those who abide in the precepts, he slanders them—such is the affliction of one engaged in worldly affairs.

Day and night there is no distinction in their thoughts; regarding food, drink, clothing, and bedding, they briefly describe these merits yet have no desire to receive them—those who engage in such activities suffer from this affliction.
One who delights in inquiring about worldly deeds and merit, who busies himself with verbal karma and finds joy therein,
yet does not revere superior virtues through diligent effort— such is the affliction of one engaged in worldly undertakings.
Addicted to construction and associating with companions, one subdues others by means of one's own power;
all manner of evil karma is thus committed—such are the afflictions of those engaged in building works.
Constantly delighting in observing the faults of others, Yet unaware of one's own transgressions and evils;
Seeing those with virtue, one always mocks them— Such are the afflictions of those engaged in worldly affairs.
Whenever I am treated with contempt by others, those who come to request the Dharma ask me to speak;
yet my intellect is not comprehensive and I lack skillful means—such are the afflictions of one engaged in worldly undertakings.
Having thus contemplated these various afflictions, those bodhisattvas who delight in this practice should perform that most excellent activity; all the deeds they perform will be without fail.
To cast away a thousand coins to take up a single coin—such a person of wisdom should be censured;
one who delights in such base occupations will be despised by others.
Therefore, the wise possess skillful means; having abandoned base and lowly occupations, the wise, once they have understood this, perform superior deeds, which are praised by all Buddhas.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those bodhisattvas lack wisdom and their mentalities are narrow and inferior; though they exert themselves with correct diligence, they abandon the most supreme Dharma and perform only minor deeds.”
The Buddha said, "Maitreya! I now inform you; I now command you."

Because those bodhisattvas have not gone forth in reliance upon the Buddha’s teaching, they are unable to extinguish [defilements]; they possess no meditative concentration, no recitation, and do not seek extensive learning.
Furthermore, Maitreya!

The Tathāgatas teach the knowledge that extinguishes conditioned activity and the wisdom that acts through knowledge; because they are fully endowed with diligent effort, they are able to discern and know this, which cannot be understood by measuring it against worldly activities.

This is not for those who exert diligent effort, nor for those who delight in hearing about the cycle of birth and death—namely, the worldly activities and the acquisition of worldly wealth—which the bodhisattva must not covet or envy.

“Maitreya! Even if a diligent bodhisattva were to construct stūpas made of the seven precious jewels filling this trichiliocosm, it could not bring me joy; it would not be an offering to me, nor would it be service rendered to me.”

Maitreya! If there should be a bodhisattva who, even with respect to a single four-line verse, receives, upholds, recites, and practices it in accordance with the pāramitās, that person shall bring me joy; they shall be making offerings to me; they shall be serving me.
Why is this so? Maitreya, it is because of their great learning; for the awakening of all Tathāgatas does not grasp at any phenomena.

“Maitreya! If there are bodhisattvas engaged in diligent activities who disturb and harass those bodhisattvas diligently engaged in study and recitation, they will cause those practicing such activities to encounter many obstacles of sin and lack any accumulation of merit.”

Why is this? Because the three kinds of supreme merit all arise from wisdom; for this reason, a bodhisattva engaged in diligent worldly activities should not obstruct other bodhisattvas who are diligently engaged in reading and reciting the scriptures.
Maitreya! It is as if all those who engage in worldly enterprises in Jambudvīpa were to fill it, their number being immeasurable;
yet one should diligently provide service to a single bodhisattva who is devoted to diligent recitation and mindfulness.
For example, suppose Jambudvīpa were filled with bodhisattvas who are diligent in recitation and mindfulness; one should serve a single person established in dhyāna-concentration.
When I say that those bodhisattvas are skillful in service, it means that such a person has already produced an immeasurable mass of merit.

Why is this so? Because this is the attainment of what is called the wisdom corresponding to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is realized as being unsurpassed; therefore, it is the most supreme, the most excellent, and the highest in all the world.
“Maitreya! For this reason, those who wish to attain meditative concentration and diligence should cultivate the work of wisdom; they should seek birth in the dwelling place of Prajñā.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

You have already explained to the bodhisattvas the faults of delighting in worldly conversation, the faults of delighting in much talk, delighting in excessive sleep, and delighting in performing many karmic actions.”
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva contemplate the delight in conceptual proliferation? Having contemplated it thus, how should they proceed toward the practice of tranquility?
The Buddha said:
“Maitreya! Those who engage in conceptual proliferation have, in brief, twenty kinds of faults that should be observed;
if explained in detail, they are infinite.”
What are these twenty?

Maitreya, bodhisattvas who engage in much conceptual proliferation find little joy in practicing the dharmas they have directly perceived; their patience further diminishes; they cultivate anger; they cause unarisen roots of goodness not to arise, and they cause already arisen roots of goodness to decline.
One will encounter strife, enmity, and resentment; one will have a short lifespan, an unattractive appearance, and stammering speech.
If the teachings of others do not abide in one's mind, the sūtras and dharmas will not manifest before one even when they have not yet been spoken.
They will be utterly estranged from all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and will quickly associate with evil associates (pāpamitra).

They shall enter the path of suffering, and at all times hear frivolous speech; wherever they are born, they will constantly fall into the net of doubt and draw near to the eight difficulties (aṣṭākṣaṇa). Within the pure dharmas, they will encounter many obstacles in their diligent pursuit of the points of training (śikṣāpada).
“Maitreya! Such as these are the twenty kinds of afflictions spoken of for bodhisattvas who engage in much conceptual proliferation.
